title: Kidney and Urinary Tract
tagline: Filtration, tubular function, fluids and electrolytes, acid–base disorders, kidney disease and the urinary tract
summary: The kidneys keep the internal environment constant. This course covers glomerular filtration and tubular function, the regulation of water, sodium, potassium, calcium and acid–base balance, acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease with dialysis, transplantation and glomerular disease, and disorders of the urinary tract.
overview: The kidneys filter about 180 litres of plasma a day and then reclaim almost all of it, adjusting the excretion of water, sodium, potassium, calcium, phosphate and acid to match intake. Because of this, nearly every acutely ill patient's fluid, electrolyte and drug-dosing problems are partly kidney problems, and much of the course is about reasoning from physiology to the bedside.

The first half is physiology applied to clinical problems. It starts with the forces that drive glomerular filtration, autoregulation, and the measurement and estimation of GFR with their traps. It then follows the filtrate along the nephron, segment by segment, explaining how each class of diuretic works and how urine is concentrated. Separate lessons treat water and sodium (hyponatraemia, hypernatraemia and safe correction rates), potassium, calcium, magnesium and phosphate, and the interpretation of blood gases with the anion gap, compensation rules and delta ratio.

The second half covers disease: acute kidney injury (KDIGO definition and staging, causes, management and the indications for dialysis), chronic kidney disease (classification, kidney-protective treatment, complications, dialysis and transplantation) with the glomerular diseases, and the urinary tract (infection, stones, obstruction, the prostate, polycystic kidney disease and urological cancers). Worked calculations of clearance, fractional excretion, water deficit, sodium correction and anion gap run through every lesson, alongside clinical cases. UK guidance (NICE, UK Kidney Association) is used where it exists, with KDIGO and European guidance where they set the standard.
outcomes: Describe the renal circulation and the glomerular filtration barrier, apply the Starling equation to glomerular filtration, and explain autoregulation and the effects of NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors on GFR.
Calculate clearance and creatinine clearance, interpret creatinine and estimated GFR, and recognise when they mislead, including in acute kidney injury and at extremes of muscle mass.
Explain transport in each segment of the nephron, the countercurrent mechanism and the action of ADH, and predict the effects of each class of diuretic and of inherited tubular disorders.
Distinguish disorders of sodium content from disorders of water balance, investigate hyponatraemia and hypernatraemia, and calculate water deficits and the safe limits of sodium correction.
Outline the regulation of potassium, calcium, magnesium and phosphate, and the recognition and principles of management of their disorders, including hyperkalaemia and refeeding syndrome.
Interpret arterial blood gases using compensation rules, the anion gap, the delta ratio and the osmolal gap, and identify mixed acid–base disorders.
Define and stage acute kidney injury using KDIGO criteria, classify its causes, outline its management and prevention, and list the indications for renal replacement therapy.
Classify chronic kidney disease by cause, GFR and albuminuria, describe treatments that slow progression, manage its complications, and outline dialysis, transplantation and conservative care.
Recognise the main glomerular diseases as nephrotic or nephritic patterns and identify rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis as an emergency.
Diagnose and outline the management of urinary tract infection, kidney stones, urinary obstruction and prostatic disease, and recognise presentations of urological cancer.

history.title: Bright's disease
history.detail: Richard Bright at Guy's Hospital links dropsy (oedema) and albumin in the urine to diseased, shrunken kidneys found at post-mortem, separating kidney disease from other causes of swelling. For a century 'Bright's disease' was the name for what is now called glomerulonephritis and chronic kidney disease.

history.title: The glomerulus described
history.detail: William Bowman describes the capillary tufts enclosed in the blind ends of the tubules, the capsule that now bears his name, and proposes that the tuft separates water from the blood.

history.title: Renin discovered
history.detail: Robert Tigerstedt and Per Bergman in Stockholm find that an extract of rabbit kidney raises blood pressure when injected into other rabbits. They name the substance renin, the first step towards the renin–angiotensin system.

history.title: Filtrate sampled
history.detail: Joseph Wearn and Alfred Richards puncture Bowman's space in frog kidneys with fine pipettes and show that the fluid is protein-free but contains glucose and chloride at plasma concentrations, proving that urine begins as an ultrafiltrate of plasma.

history.title: Goldblatt hypertension
history.detail: Harry Goldblatt narrows the renal arteries of dogs with an adjustable clamp and produces sustained hypertension, showing that reduced kidney perfusion raises blood pressure. The work led to the identification of angiotensin by Irvine Page and by Eduardo Braun-Menéndez and colleagues in 1939–40.

history.title: The first successful dialysis
history.detail: Willem Kolff, who had built a rotating-drum artificial kidney in the occupied Netherlands from 1943, treats a woman with acute kidney failure who survives, the first patient saved by dialysis. Long-term dialysis became possible after Belding Scribner's arteriovenous shunt in 1960.

history.title: The countercurrent multiplier
history.detail: Bartholomew Hargitay and Werner Kuhn propose that the hairpin loop of Henle multiplies a small single effect into a large osmotic gradient, and with Heinrich Wirz demonstrate the rising osmolality from cortex to papilla in rat kidney slices.

history.title: The first successful kidney transplant
history.detail: On 23 December 1954, at the Peter Bent Brigham Hospital in Boston, Joseph Murray, John Merrill and Hartwell Harrison transplant a kidney from Ronald Herrick into his identical twin Richard. Without rejection, the kidney works for years. Murray later shared the 1990 Nobel Prize.

history.title: Inappropriate antidiuretic hormone
history.detail: William Schwartz, Frederic Bartter and colleagues describe two patients with lung cancer, hyponatraemia, concentrated urine and continued urinary sodium loss, and attribute it to inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone.

history.title: Erythropoietin for kidney failure
history.detail: Joseph Eschbach and colleagues show that recombinant human erythropoietin, cloned by Fu-Kuen Lin's group in 1985, corrects the anaemia of people on dialysis, replacing one of the kidney's hormonal functions. Later trials showed that aiming for a normal haemoglobin increased cardiovascular events, which is why targets are set below normal.

references.title: Renal Physiology
references.authors: Bruce M. Koeppen and Bruce A. Stanton
references.note: Sixth edition (Mosby Physiology series). A short, clear account of filtration, tubular transport and the regulation of body fluids; the best companion to the physiology lessons.
